title: DNS & HTTP: From a URL to a Web Page
oneLiner: Typing a URL and seeing a page triggers a whole chain of lookups and handshakes underneath -- this is that chain, one step at a time.
keyTakeaway: DNS turns a name into an address (Application layer asking the Internet layer's addressing system a question); the TCP handshake and, for HTTPS, the TLS handshake happen BEFORE any actual HTTP request goes out; and the whole sequence repeats for every extra resource a page needs, often reusing the same already-open connection instead of paying for a new handshake each time.
explanation:
Typing a URL and pressing enter looks instant, but it's really a chain of separate steps across several layers (see The OSI & TCP/IP Models). First, DNS: the browser needs an IP address to actually connect to (see IP Addressing & Subnetting), so it asks a DNS resolver "what's the IP for this hostname?" -- checking its own cache first, since re-asking for a name it already resolved recently would be wasted round-trips. Once it has an IP, it opens a TCP connection to it (see TCP vs UDP) via the three-way handshake, and for HTTPS, layers a TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption behind HTTPS) handshake on top of that to agree on encryption BEFORE any real HTTP data is exchanged -- that's why HTTPS's first request has more round-trip overhead than plain HTTP, encryption isn't free at connection-open time.

Only after both handshakes complete does the browser send the actual HTTP request -- a method and path (GET /path HTTP/1.1) plus headers like Host and User-Agent -- and the server sends back a response: a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 301 Redirect, ...), response headers, and the actual content. If that content is an HTML page, the browser then parses it, finds every additional resource it references (images, stylesheets, scripts), and repeats the DNS-then-connect-then-request sequence for each one -- though modern HTTP reuses an already-open TCP connection for multiple requests to the same server rather than paying for a fresh handshake every single time, which is a large part of why sites with many small resources on the same domain load faster than the same total data spread across many different domains.
